about: Keep Calm and Carry On is the blank red version of the famous British poster: a flat red rectangle with the white Tudor-style crown at the top and plenty of space below it for the slogan. The original message was stiff-upper-lip encouragement for a country expecting war, and its calm, official look is what makes it easy to parody. People keep the "Keep Calm and..." formula and replace the ending with something silly, nerdy or completely the opposite of calm.
origin: The poster was designed in 1939 by the British Ministry of Information but was barely displayed at the time. A copy found at Barter Books in Alnwick in 2000 led to reprints, and in the late 2000s it became a hugely popular design and parody format.
usage:
This template has one large box under the crown. Write the whole poster text there, traditionally in three or four short lines: "keep calm and" followed by your own instruction.

The parody works by keeping the official tone while the advice becomes absurd, overly specific, or a bad idea in disguise. Coding (push to production), studying (pretend you read it), gaming (blame lag) and sports (trust the process) all work. Keep it short; the real poster has only five words.
